analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent commission to identify and recommend terminating unfair federal corporate subsidies and tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for any vote: it sat in the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee for over a year, with no markup, until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a nine-member Corporate Subsidy Reform Commission to comb through federal programs and tax laws and identify subsidies that hand money or tax advantages to for-profit businesses without a public benefit in return. Like the military base-closing commissions, its recommendations would go to the President, who could approve or reject them, and any approved package would get fast-track treatment in Congress with limited debate and strict amendment rules. The commission would have expired in 2002.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently fund payments, benefits, and tax advantages to businesses that the bill's own findings call unnecessary or unjustified windfalls. Honest businesses that compete without federal help would also benefit from a fairer playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares it unfair to force taxpayers to support subsidies, including tax advantages, that provide no substantial public benefit, and directs the commission to identify and recommend terminating or reforming them [S2][S3].

The process is designed to break gridlock: after the President approves the commission's package, Congress must introduce implementing bills within 14 days, committees must report within 120 days or lose the bill, and floor debate is capped, so individual subsidy beneficiaries could not stall it indefinitely [S3].

Every recommendation would be judged against a public test: a subsidy is 'inequitable' only if it gives no public return at least as great as its cost and confers an unfair competitive advantage or windfall [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and industries receiving the targeted subsidies would lose payments, benefits, and tax advantages. Workers and communities tied to those subsidized industries could face job losses as the support ends. Federal agencies running the programs would lose them.

drawbacks.text: The bill concentrates major spending decisions in an unelected, nine-member commission whose package Congress must consider under fast-track rules with sharply limited debate and amendment, trading away normal legislative deliberation to overcome gridlock [S3].

The bill builds in a large escape hatch: any bill referred to the tax committees that raises revenue by ending subsidies could be amended to include tax cuts of up to the same amount, and unmade cuts would be credited to the pay-as-you-go scorecard — meaning savings could flow back out as tax cuts rather than deficit reduction [S3].

The scope is narrower than the title suggests: subsidies for research and development, programs primarily benefiting public health, safety, the environment, or education, trade-obligation payments, and programs certified by the Trade Representative are all exempt from review [S3].
The bill only studies and recommends — no subsidy is cut unless the President approves the package and Congress passes implementing legislation, so the actual savings were always uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real value was procedural: bundling subsidy terminations into an up-or-down package is the only design that has historically overcome the protective grip each subsidy's beneficiaries hold over Congress. Its weaknesses are real — an unelected commission operating under fast-track rules, big carve-outs, and a tax-cut offset that could swallow the savings — but the bill itself cost taxpayers almost nothing, while its death left every unfair subsidy in place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee in November 1999 and never got a markup or vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: McCain introduced the bill on November 19, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S5].

On February 2, 2000, the Senate ordered that if the Governmental Affairs Committee ever reported the bill, it would then go to the Finance Committee for up to 45 session days — a sign leadership wanted it alive, since nothing ever came out of either committee [S5][S3].
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill dead [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and industries receiving federal subsidies and tax advantages kept every dollar untouched, because a commission that might have recommended terminating them was never allowed to exist. Taxpayers gained nothing.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill during the roughly 13 months remaining in the Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican lead sponsor with two Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — and no opposition ever went on the record, because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Corporations receiving federal subsidies and tax advantages
industries.note: The bill's whole purpose is to terminate payments, benefits, and tax advantages to for-profit businesses that return no public benefit and confer unfair windfalls [S2][S3]. Every dollar such a business keeps is a cost the taxpayer bears.

industries.industry: Recipients of shielded subsidies (research and development, health, safety, environment, education, trade programs)
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts merit-based R&D, programs primarily benefiting public health, safety, the environment, or education, trade-obligation payments, and programs certified by the Trade Representative, locking those subsidies out of any review [S3]. Some genuinely serve the public; the carve-out also means the commission could never touch them regardless of performance.
